newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Michael Jackson reported not a hit at APEC.
newsitem.headline: Michael Jackson reported not a hit at APEC.

text.p: Michael Jackson is getting bad press at the Asia-Pacific summit.

As the pop icon was enjoying his honeymoon he probably was blissfully unaware that Philippine newspaper People's Tonight was conducting a poll on his popularity among delegates preparing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
It found "an overwhelming consensus" against Jackson's Philippine concert next month.
It quoted an APEC issues consultant from Jackson's home country, the United States, as saying it was a moral question.
"The point is the American people have changed a lot by changing their moral values," Steven Earl Drice, 35, was quoted as saying.
"This includes attending bible studies, other related movements and charismatic occasions or activities instead of concentrating on unnecessary entertainment."
Old protectionist habits die hard among leaders here to build the world's biggest free trade zone, according to Philippine Star columnist Max V. Soliven.
He said President Bill Clinton had rejected an official bullet-proof Mercedes for driving around the summit site at Subic Bay in favour of an American car.
"Let's face it, sloganeering is fine, but when push comes to shove nationalism always prevails," he sniffed.

Leftist protesters crying that APEC is merely a vehicle for American corporations to dominate the region were fed fuel for their cause by the official list of delegates to the APEC Business Forum, set up to turn political promise into hard contracts.
The United States sent 173 businessmen, four times as many as the next biggest team, from Japan. China, the most populous APEC member and contender for the title of 21st century superpower, sent 21.
Security was so tight when Clinton flew in that the Secret Service which looks after American presidents stopped Philippine Vice President Joseph Estrada when he went to Manila airport to meet him.
"You cannot tell me what to do right here in my country," Estrada snapped to the security men. "I am the vice president."
He was allowed through.

Four unwary pedestrians have been killed so far trying to cross the "friendship lanes" set up to speed delegates and other visitors to pre-summit conferences through Manila's notoriously clogged streets.

The "friendship lanes", which are empty most of the time, have been causing severe attacks of road rage among Filipino drivers squeezed into enormous traffic jams in what remains of their roads as the APEC VIPs cruise comfortably by.
APEC now has an anthem.
"Come share the dream," goes the refrain of the hymn "A New Liberty", composed by Philippine Foreign Undersecretary Federico Macarenos.
Verse Three sums it up:
"United by an ocean great
Fervid ideals thrown to fate
To lead the next millennium
Economies cooperate."
He inspected the bathrooms, fussed around the carpet fitters, eyed the shrubbery and checked out the golf course.

And, after he had poked around the Subic Bay site of this year's APEC summit, President Fidel Ramos, playing concerned host ahead of the arrival of world leaders, pronounced the venue "better than all the others".
Better than last year at the Japanese city of Osaka with its medieval castle, better than Bogor in Indonesia in 1994 when delegates sported hand-printed batik shirts.
Ramos paused at a jungle opening to observe some sleeping monkeys.
"This reminds me of my cabinet," he quipped.
Christmas carols jingled through Manila airport as summiteers flew into the most faithful Roman Catholic country in Asia.
"God rest ye Merry Gentlemen, may nothing you dismay..." they were advised as they prepared to wrestle with the fate of a region that accounts for more than half the world's economic output.
